14054-max:
Katherine Cecil Thurston published Max in 1910, a novel of art, identity, and Paris. Max, a mysterious artist, draws two souls together in subtle fusion. Illustrations by Frank Craig picture Petersburg courts, a waiting lifetime, and a woman's complete semblance. A night journey opens part one, with a mask of immobility falling on a hero's face.

Thurston, author of The Masquerader, builds the plot on disguise, genius, and love. Max's art dazzles: why, boy, this is clever, a watcher cries. French phrases on eternal, all-powerful life punctuate the romance. The novel mixes society drama with artistic mystery. It suits readers of Edwardian romantic fiction.
16080-uncle-max:
Rosa Nouchette Carey's 1894 domestic novel Uncle Max opens out of the mist and behind the bars, with a Cinderella figure and an uncle who breaks the ice. Later chapters visit the White Cottage, meet Giles Hamilton, raise a flag of truce, and nurse a difficult patient, before Lady Betty, Gladys, and the mystery at Gladwyn take center stage. A runaway, a blackened memory, and a captain's story deepen the plot.

Carey, author of Nellie's Memories and Wee Wifie, writes warm, respectable tales of family, duty, and love rewarded. Her heroines suffer patiently, her villains scheme quietly, and her endings restore order. Readers of Victorian domestic fiction will find this a gentle, absorbing story of home and heart.
17086-the-vicissitudes-of-bessie-fairfax:
Holme Lee, pen name of Harriet Parr, tells Bessie Fairfax's long life from birth and parentage through exile, school at Caen, and a family secret learned at last. A lawyer's letter, a ride with the doctor, and friends at Brook and Beechhurst shape her youth, while later chapters bring Brentwood dinners, Minster Court, and Bessie's own peacemaking. The novel runs to more than forty chapters.

Parr writes in the full Victorian domestic mode, with kin, class, and marriage as its stakes. Bessie grows from a girl acted upon to a woman who shows character and settles others' quarrels. Fans of long, earnest Victorian novels will find a rich, patient story of a woman's fortunes and heart.
2348-the-disappearance-of-lady-frances-c:
Holmes is called to find Lady Frances Carfax, a lonely aristocrat who has vanished on the Continent, leaving only a trail of hotels and a coffin. Arthur Conan Doyle sends Watson ahead to investigate, then brings Holmes to rescue the lady from a villainous couple's murderous plot. The story's tension builds through Watson's reports from abroad.

The case turns on a false funeral and a race against burial alive. It is a late Holmes adventure with real suspense. Readers will enjoy Watson's unusually central role. Watson's solo work in this case shows how much he learned from Holmes.
31990-a-history-of-the-town-of-fairfax:
Jeanne Johnson Rust's History of the Town of Fairfax, published in 1960 and illustrated by Paul R. Hoffmaster, is dedicated to her husband and his favorite town, his birthplace. Its map legend guides a reader through Fairfax landmarks, from the court house and Duncan's Chapel to Payne's Church, the Ford Building, Rose Bower, the site of Willcoxon Tavern, and Truro Church.

The volume, printed by Moore and Moore of Washington, is a local history built from records, buildings, and memory. Readers get a mid-twentieth-century town chronicle, useful for anyone tracing Fairfax families, churches, and streets through Virginia history.
48834-the-great-diamond-hoax:
The Great Diamond Hoax and Other Stirring Incidents in the Life of Asbury Harpending is a memoir edited by James Wilkins and copyrighted in 1913 at San Francisco. A front portrait shows Harpending at seventy six, in June 1915. His preface says plain duty to his family name forced the book.

In the famous diamond fraud of the 1870s, salted mines fooled leading financiers, and later writers named Harpending as a plotter. He insists he was only a dupe like the rest, and prints one historian's apology. Early California tales fill out the volume. It is self defense, but lively and close to the events.
62779-the-moon-hoax:
Richard Adams Locke wrote The Moon Hoax, a famous set of fake reports that claimed the moon has a vast population of human beings. A plate shows the moon as seen by Lord Rosse's telescope in 1856. A quoted passage at the front describes an ocean planted with islands, covered with fruits and flowers and shining seas.

Locke first ran the tales in a New York newspaper as real news from a great telescope in South Africa. Readers believed in bat men, temples, and beasts on the moon, until the joke came out. The book preserves the full hoax. Readers now get to enjoy the prose that fooled a city, and to judge its craft.
68586-smoking-flax:
Smoking Flax, by Hallie Erminie Rives, reached a second edition from Neely of London and New York. Its copyright dates to 1897. Rives gives the book to her mother and the South. An introduction calls it a story of the South by a young Kentucky woman. It warns that the North may receive the book in a harder spirit. The subject, it says, assures close attention in any case.

The theme is lynch law, named there as the methods of Judge Lynch. The introduction grants that such acts look evil from most standpoints. From a few aspects, it claims, they may seem partly excused. Rives presents the question through romance, from many sides. She leaves the verdict on truth to the reader, though her own sympathies show plainly.
britannica-1911-addax:
Addax is a genus of antelopes with one species. North Africa and Arabia form its range. The animal stands a little over three feet high. Its colour is yellowish white overall. A brown mane marks its neck and head. A fringe of the same hue hangs on its throat. Both sexes carry horns in this species. The horns are ringed along their length. They form an open spiral as they grow.

Desert life shapes the addax wholly. Its habits probably resemble the gemsbuck's closely. Arabs hunt it for its flesh. They also hunt it to test horses and greyhounds. Speed trials against their animals are the point. Young addaxes are captured during these hunting parties. Menageries receive the captured young for display.
britannica-1911-anthrax:
Anthrax is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a sharp, deadly disease. The Greek name means coal, since the sore was thought to burn like coal. A germ named in the text is given as its cause. It strikes beasts most, chiefly cattle, sheep, and horses.

Men who work with wool, hair, hides, or dead beasts can catch it too. The entry says the disease is spread wide across the globe. It kills reindeer herds in Lapland and is known in hot and mild lands alike. A long list of lands where it has been seen is given. Marshy ground and tight subsoil are linked to its worst visits.
britannica-1911-anticlimax:
An anticlimax, in the art of speech, is a sharp drop from a high pitch of thought to a low one. The speaker or writer seems to aim at a grand point, then falls off in a flat or small close. The 1911 Britannica entry gives the term as the reverse of climax, and shows it in a famed mock couplet.

A great lord is named as a god of war in one line, the entry quotes. The next line drops him to a mere deputy rank in a peers train. Such a drop can be used on purpose only for a joke or a jab, the entry says. It often takes the form of a sharp contrast of grand and base. The piece ends by parting the term from bathos: a whole speech may wallow in bathos, but a drop needs a rise to fall from.
britannica-1911-borax:
Borax is a sodium borate salt sold in two forms, and the entry is a full chemical and mineral account of it. Common or prismatic borax carries ten parts of water in its crystals, while jewellers' or octahedral borax carries five. The old alchemists used the name loosely, the entry warns, not always for this substance.

Natural borax turns up in Tibet, Canada, Peru, and Transylvania, and a great crust of it at Borax Lake in California could be used by the assayer with no cleaning at all. Most supply, though, was made from Tuscan boric acid fused with sodium carbonate, or from natural calcium borate. The pages that follow treat its uses in glass, enamel, soldering, and medicine, and its mineral sources.
britannica-1911-bruch-max:
Max Bruch (born 1838) was a German composer born at Cologne on 6 January 1838, son of a city official and grandson of the famed Evangelical cleric Dr Christian Bruch. His mother, a well-known musician of her time, taught him music's elements, but under Breidenstein he made his first serious effort at fourteen, producing a symphony.

In 1853 he won the Mozart Stipendium of 400 gulden a year for four years at Frankfort, then studied under Hiller, Reinecke and Breunung. He taught piano at Cologne from 1858 to 1861, where his one-act opera Scherz, List und Rache was produced in 1858. His father's death in 1861 began years of study travel through Berlin, Leipzig, Vienna, Munich, Dresden and Mannheim. His opera Lorelei came out in 1863 and where he wrote the beautiful Frithjof. Posts as musical director at Coblenz and court conductor at Sondershausen followed, then Berlin, where he wrote his Odysseus and his first violin work.
britannica-1911-flax:
Flax, or lint, names both a fibre and the plant it comes from. The flax plant, Linum usitatissimum, belongs to the family Linaceae. Long cultivation has produced many varieties, and its wild origin is doubtful. As grown it is an annual with an erect stalk 20 to 40 inches high. Narrow leaves sit along the stalk, and each top branch ends in a bright blue flower. Its round fruit holds ten cells, each with a single seed.

Those seeds are linseed, heavy, smooth and glossy, and rich in oil of great trade value. The long article follows the plant into the field and the mill. It treats the fibre in the stem, how flax is raised, pulled, retted and dressed, and what the fibre and seed are used for. Few farm plants of the age matched flax, giving linen fibre from the stalk and oil from the seed in one crop.
britannica-1911-hierax:
Hierax, or Hieracas, was a learned ascetic who flourished about the end of the 3rd century at Leontopolis in Egypt. He lived to ninety, supporting himself by calligraphy and studying in his spare time, above all the Bible. He wrote commentaries in Greek and Coptic. He led the sect called the Hieracites.

That sect shut out married persons, holding that only the celibate could enter the kingdom of heaven. Hierax taught that suppressing the sexual impulse was the new revelation brought by the Logos. He is called the link between Origen and the Coptic monks, a man of deep learning and vast memory. He figured the Son as a torch lit at the torch of the Father. He denied a bodily resurrection and a material paradise. He also doubted the salvation of baptized infants, since without knowledge there is no conflict and no reward.
britannica-1911-hipponax:
Hipponax of Ephesus, a Greek iambic poet, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The tyrant Athenagoras drove him from Ephesus in 540 BC. He found refuge at Clazomenae, where he spent the rest of his life in poverty. No dates of birth or death are given in the short piece.

His bent figure and spiteful temper drew the mockery of two sculptors of Chios. They carved him in caricature, and he answered with a stream of satires. The pair are said to have hanged themselves under that attack. The article judges his work coarse in thought and rude in speech. Local allusions crowd it, and it never won favour in Attica. Still, he is credited with inventing parody as a form. He also devised a limping verse measure, the scazon, fit for the burlesque tone of his poems.
britannica-1911-lesbonax: Lesbonax of Mytilene was a Greek speaker and teacher of speech in the age of Augustus. Photius credits him with sixteen speeches on public affairs. Two still survive. One urges Athens against Sparta in the manner of Thucydides. The other, under a false title, speaks on the Corinthian War against Thebes. Letters of love also bear his name. Two other men blur the record: an older Lesbonax with many works on deep thought, and a later one with a small piece on turns of phrase.
britannica-1911-o-rell-max:
Max O'Rell was the pen name of Paul Blouet, who lived from 1848 to 1903. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica presents this French writer as a wit on two shores. Born in Brittany, he served as a cavalry officer in the war with Germany. He was taken at Sedan, freed, then badly wounded in the Paris fighting. In 1872 he went to England as a news writer. From 1876 he taught French at St Paul's school in London.

His first book, John Bull and his Island, made his pen name a household word. It was read widely in French and in English. More books in the same vein treated Scotland, America, and France. His wife, an Englishwoman, translated his work. From 1890 his main work was lecturing. His easy manner and humour packed halls in Britain and America.
britannica-1911-parallax:
Parallax is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a term in astronomy. The Greek root of the word means alternately. It names the apparent change in a body's direction. That change appears when the body is viewed from two different points. Geocentric parallax is the angle between two such directions. One is seen from the surface of the earth. The other is the direction from the earth's centre.

Annual parallax is the like angle for a star. The other is the direction from the centre of the sun. The solar parallax is discussed below in the entry. The problem of the sun's distance has always been fundamental. It is the fundamental problem of celestial measurement, the text says. The difficulties in the way of solving it are very great. The best authorities are not agreed as to the result.
britannica-1911-wax: Wax is a solid fatty substance of animal and vegetable origin, allied to oils and fats. It stands apart from oils and fats in one clear point of makeup. Oils and fats are glycerides, built with glycerin as one part. A true wax holds no glycerin in its makeup at all. It joins fatty acids with certain solid alcohols instead of glycerin. The entry sends readers to the article on oils for the wider account of these substances and their kin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abrasax:
Abrasax is the true name, not Abraxas, of a class of small ancient stones carved with strange figures and formulas. Many of them still resist interpretation, and specimens sit in almost every museum and private collection. The spelling Abraxas arose from Latin confusion between Sigma and Xi. Among early Gnostics the word carried several meanings, and Basilides gave the title to Almighty God, claiming its letters add up to 365, the number of the solar cycle.

It is an error, the entry insists, to call every Gnostic stone an Abrasax, just as Jupiter and Venus do not name every ancient statue. Abrasax names the Supreme Deity in Gnostic thought, not talismans in general. Very many secrets of Gnosticism remain unexplained, the entry admits, but hopes they will not stay shrouded in mystery. It points readers to King, Bellermann, Dieterich, and Matter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dax:
A diocesan entry describes Dax, an ancient French see suppressed under the Concordat of 1801, its territory now split between Aix and Bayonne. Its patron, the martyr Vincent, may not have been a bishop, though his cult existed in Charlemagne's time. The oldest martyrdom account comes from a thirteenth-century Dax breviary, and excavations found a Merovingian cemetery on a church site dedicated to Vincent by Bishop Gratianus.

Gratianus, present at Agde in 506, is the first historically known bishop. Later bishops included Revellatus, Macarius, and Cardinals Itier and Foix, founder of Avignon University and Toulouse's College de Foix. Dax's synodal constitutions, published by Abbe Degert, illuminate thirteenth- and fourteenth-century church customs, and Vincent de Paul first studied there with the Cordeliers about 1588.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-halifax:
Nova Scotia's Archdiocese of Halifax takes its name from the capital founded by Lord Cornwallis in 1749 and covers the province's middle and western counties with Bermuda, attached since 1851. Its story opens at Port Royal, founded by De Monts in 1604. Mass was first offered there on what is now Canadian soil.

French Jesuits, Recollects, and Capuchins worked among settlers and Micmacs until the Acadian expulsion of 1755, and penal laws kept Catholics down until Irish petitioners won repeal in 1783. A vicariate in 1817 became a diocese in 1842 and an archdiocese in 1852, under bishops Burke, Fraser, Walsh, and Connolly, the last a champion of confederation and foe of Fenianism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maximinus-thr:
Maximinus Thrax, Roman emperor from 235 to 238, was the son of a Goth and an Alanic mother. A shepherd of huge size and strength, he caught Septimius Severus's eye in a contest with soldiers during the emperor's passage through Thrace in 202 and joined the body-guard. He refused to serve under Macrinus and Heliogabalus, but Alexander Severus gave him command of new Pannonian troops.

Those troops, wanting a real warrior rather than the timid young Alexander, ruled by his mother Julia Mamaea, proclaimed Maximinus emperor at Mainz in March 235, with his son Maximus as co-regent. He campaigned with vigour across the Rhine, regained the Agri Decumates, and beat Sarmatians and Dacians on the Danube, taking the names Germanicus and Sarmaticus. He taxed and executed patricians freely, melted temple bronze for coin, and showered revenues on his devoted soldiers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pax:
Pax, also called osculatorium or tabula pacis, is a tablet for giving the peace. The Church's primitive usage was the holy kiss given freely. Later, under the Apostolic Constitutions, lay men kissed men and women kissed women. That lasted till the thirteenth century, when a substitute appeared: a tablet or plate bearing the Blessed Virgin, the church's titular, or most often the crucifixion.

The earliest notice of them lies in thirteenth-century English council records. Cardinal Bona credits the Franciscans with the departure. Kissed by the celebrant and wiped with linen, the tablet was carried to others to kiss. The rite holds in low Masses, giving peace to prelates and princes, rarely to others by custom. The acolyte at the celebrant's right presents the tablet. The celebrant kisses it saying Peace be with you. The server answers, And with your spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pertinax:
Pertinax was a Roman emperor whose reign lasted barely three months in 193. A freedman's son born at Alba Pompeia in 126, he taught grammar at Rome before joining the army. Ability in war and civil office won him praetorship, consulship, and commands along the Danube under Marcus Aurelius, governorships of Moesia, Dacia, and Syria, and later the prefecture of Rome under Commodus.

After Commodus was strangled, soldiers proclaimed Pertinax emperor at the praetorian prefect's urging, and the Senate confirmed him. He revived the title Princeps Senatus and took the name Father of his Country. Selling Commodus's costly plate and furniture, he paid the guards, resumed public works, recalled the banished, and tried informers. He died at Rome on 28 March 193, after ruling from the last day of 192.
doe-osti-2997461-variable-curvature-pult:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory final report ORNL/TM-2025/4185, by Jim Tobin and Ian Brownstein, dated September 2025, closes cooperative project NFE-24-10099 on blades for vertical axis wind turbines. Vertical turbines spin around an upright shaft, and their blades curve along their length. Pultrusion, pulling fiber through a shaping die, makes long constant-section parts cheaply, but a varying curve fights that process.

Tasks developed conceptual blade designs rated at 15 megawatts, then costed them. Partner XFlow produced a glass fiber design; a carbon fiber variant was dropped on cost grounds. Cost estimates built on the surviving glass design feed the next decision round. The filing records design intent and economics for a blade style that could suit large offshore vertical machines, where pultruded construction would cut manufacturing cost per blade.
doe-osti-3002125-variable-curvature-pult: Wind blades got variably curved, and this DOE text covers pultruded vertical axis designs. The pages detail the findings. The wind folks get their data. The blades were vertical axis. The designs were pultruded. The folks were wind. The data were blade.
max: Katherine Cecil Thurston wrote Max, a novel printed by Harper in 1910. Frank Craig drew the pictures, and one shows a figure in a Petersburg court. The hosted sample preserves the front pages and the picture list only. No readable chapter text appears beyond the head of part one. This note stays with the title, the author, and the year for that reason. The plot cannot be described from the sample held here.
nasa-tm-19720024218-a-model-of-the-local: A model of the local region of the galaxy is a NASA technical memorandum on space near the Sun. The hosted sample is garbled optical character text, and it preserves no readable author name, center, or date. Its abstract, kept with the record, describes a two part model of matter between the stars. The model rests on low radio waves picked up by the Radio Astronomy Explorer satellite. It points to a thick spiral arm and a thick layer tied to electrons.
the-disappearance-of-lady-frances-carfax:
Sir Arthur Conan Doyle opens The Disappearance of Lady Frances Carfax on a small deduction. But why Turkish? asks Sherlock Holmes, gazing fixedly at Watson's boots, as Watson reclines in a cane-backed chair with his feet out. Watson answers that the boots are English, bought at Latimer's in Oxford Street.

Holmes corrects him: he meant the bath. Why the relaxing, costly Turkish bath rather than the brisk home-made kind? Watson pleads rheumatism and age; a Turkish bath is an alterative, a fresh starting-point, a cleanser of the system. He then asks Holmes to show the link between boots and bath. Holmes points to splashes on the left sleeve and shoulder of Watson's coat. Had he sat in the center of a hansom, the splashes would be few or balanced. So he sat at the side, and he had a companion in the cab that morning.
the-vicissitudes-of-bessie-fairfax: Holme Lee, the pen name of Harriet Parr, wrote The Vicissitudes of Bessie Fairfax, issued at Philadelphia by Porter and Coates. An epigraph warns that life gives not what we wish but what we must put up with. Only the title page and a partial contents list are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. Chapters trace Bessie's birth and parentage, a lawyer's letter, the community of Beechhurst, and a fate sealed against her inclination. Later headings promise school-days at Caen and a family secret.
uncle-max: Rosa Nouchette Carey's Uncle Max, dated 1894, survives here through its contents. The chapters open Out of the Mist, then move behind bars to a Cinderella, and Uncle Max breaks the ice in chapter four. Later titles promise a flag of truce, a difficult patient, one of God's heroines, and a missed vocation. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
